theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: A price list says "Cable ties, 100/pk". What does "pk" mean?

A breaker's breaking capacity is given as 10 kA. What does "kA" stand for?
A supplier's email gives the "ETA" of a delivery. What do the letters ETA stand for?

essays.stem: From the drawings, schedules and specification for a two-storey medical centre, explain how you would build a bill of materials and turn it into orders that can be called off as the job proceeds.
essays.modelAnswer: I would make sure I have the latest revision of every drawing, the fittings and board schedules, and the specification. I would split the job into sections, such as containment, cabling, wiring accessories, lighting, distribution and special systems, and take off each one floor by floor. I would count accessories and fittings from the plans and schedules, and measure cable and conduit runs to scale, adding drops, rises and tails, then a waste allowance. Each line would get its full description, part number, rating and unit of measure from the specification. I would check the store for usable stock. Then I would match the bill of materials to the job programme: items needed early, such as conduit, boxes and trunking, go on the first orders; long-lead items, such as boards and special fittings, are ordered early but called off later; and second-fix items are called off floor by floor. Each order would carry the job number, delivery dates and site contact, and the totals would be checked by a second person.
markingPoints: Uses the latest drawings, schedules and specification
Takes off by section and floor, measuring runs with drops and waste
Full description, part number, rating and unit for each line
Checks existing stock
Splits into orders and call-offs matched to the programme, with long-lead items early; checked

essays.stem: For each of these items, list the details an order must give and say what could go wrong if one is missing: armoured cable, a distribution board with breakers, outdoor floodlights, and a 220 V pump motor.
essays.modelAnswer: For armoured cable the order must give the conductor size, number of cores, conductor material, insulation type, armour type, voltage rating, length and whether it is on a drum or cut lengths. If the cores or material are missing, the wrong cable may come and not suit the glands or the load. For a distribution board it must give the number of ways, main switch rating, busbar rating, single or three phase, the breaking capacity, and each breaker's rating, poles and type, plus any RCDs. A missing breaking capacity could give breakers too weak for the fault level. For outdoor floodlights it must give the wattage, light output, colour temperature, beam angle, voltage, IP rating and mounting. Without the IP rating, fittings may let in water and fail. For a pump motor it must give the power, voltage, 50 Hz frequency, phases, speed, frame size, mounting and enclosure rating. A wrong voltage or frequency would make the motor run badly or burn out.
markingPoints: Cable details (size, cores, material, insulation, armour, voltage, length)
Board details (ways, ratings, phases, breaking capacity, breakers, RCDs)
Floodlight details including IP rating and voltage
Motor details including voltage, 50 Hz, power, phases and mounting
Says what goes wrong when a detail is missing

essays.stem: Describe how you would set up and run an order schedule (order tracker) for a commercial electrical job: what columns it holds, how long-lead items are handled and how you keep it up to date.
essays.modelAnswer: I would set up a shared spreadsheet with one row for each order line or package. The columns would be: item and specification reference, quantity and unit, supplier, requisition number, purchase order number, date ordered, lead time, date needed on site from the programme, the latest order date, promised delivery date, actual delivery date, the quantity received, any shortage or damage, and notes. I would sort it by the date needed. Long-lead items, such as the main switchboard, generator changeover switch and special fittings, would be marked so they stand out, ordered as soon as their design is approved, and chased each week. I would update the tracker whenever an order is placed, confirmed, delivered or changed, and check it every week against the programme with the site supervisor. Any item at risk of arriving late would be raised at once so the plan can change, and the finished tracker would be kept with the job file.
markingPoints: Shared tracker with one row per order line
Sensible columns: references, quantities, supplier, PO, dates ordered, needed and delivered, receipts
Long-lead items marked, ordered early and chased
Updated at every change and reviewed weekly with the site
Late risks raised early; tracker kept with the job file

essays.stem: A supplier warns that the main switchboard for a school will arrive four weeks late. Explain what you would do.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would get the facts in writing from the supplier: the reason, the new date, and whether part of the order could come sooner. I would tell the site supervisor and project manager straight away and look at the programme to see what work depends on the board, such as terminating sub-mains, testing and the inspection before connection. I would look for options: another approved supplier with a board in stock that meets the specification, a different make approved by the designer, a faster shipping method, or a temporary supply arranged with the client. Any change of make would need written approval. With the site team I would re-plan the work so other tasks, such as containment, wiring and final circuits, carry on while we wait. I would tell the client about any effect on the finish date. I would then chase the supplier every week, record every contact on the order tracker, and note the supplier's performance for future orders.
markingPoints: Gets the details and new date in writing
Informs site and project managers and checks what work depends on it
Looks for alternatives: other approved suppliers, approved substitutes, faster shipping
Re-plans work and informs the client
Chases and records progress; notes supplier performance

essays.stem: Describe how you would train a site storeman to receive deliveries of cable, boards and fittings, including what to check, what to sign and what to record.
essays.modelAnswer: I would show him how to find the purchase order before the truck arrives, so he knows what to expect. When the goods come, he checks the delivery note against the order: item, part number, quantity and unit. For cable he reads the sheath printing for size, cores, type and voltage, and checks the drum for damage and the length. For boards he checks the ratings plate, number of ways, breakers and any damage to the door and busbars. For fittings he counts the boxes, opens a sample and checks the wattage, voltage and IP rating. He then signs the delivery note only for what has actually arrived, writing any shortage, wrong item or damage on it before signing, with photos. He records the delivery on the goods received record and tracker, with batch numbers, and tells the buyer about any problem the same day. Damaged or wrong goods are labelled and kept apart. Finally he stores the goods correctly and safely, using team lifts or equipment for heavy items.
markingPoints: Gets the purchase order ready before delivery
Checks delivery note against the order
Checks specific details for cable, boards and fittings
Signs only for what arrived, noting shortages and damage, with photos
Records receipt and batches, reports problems, quarantines and stores safely

essays.stem: Explain how minimum, maximum and reorder levels work for a contractor's store of common electrical items. Give an example calculation.
essays.modelAnswer: The minimum (safety) level is the stock kept to cover late deliveries or extra use, so the store should rarely fall below it. The reorder level is the point at which a new order is placed. It must cover the stock used while waiting for the delivery, plus the safety stock: reorder level = use during the lead time + safety stock. The maximum level is the most that should be held, so money and space are not tied up and items do not get old or damaged. The order quantity is roughly the maximum less the stock left when the new goods arrive. For example, the store uses about 40 boxes of wire connectors a month, delivery takes half a month, and the safety stock is 15 boxes. The reorder level is 20 + 15 = 35 boxes. If the maximum is 80 boxes, when stock reaches 35 the buyer orders about 80 − 15 = 65 boxes, because about 20 will be used before the delivery arrives. Levels are reviewed when use changes.
markingPoints: Explains minimum (safety) stock
Explains reorder level = use in lead time + safety stock
Explains maximum level and why it matters
Correct example calculation
Levels reviewed when use or lead time changes

essays.stem: Explain how changes to orders should be handled when the design changes or a supplier offers a substitute, and why approval and records matter.
essays.modelAnswer: When the design changes, the buyer should get the revised drawing or written instruction first, then check which orders are affected. If the goods have not shipped, he asks the supplier to amend the order and gets a revised confirmation in writing. If they have shipped, he agrees returns or a restocking charge, or decides with the site whether the old items can be used elsewhere. When a supplier offers a substitute, the buyer gets its data sheet and compares it with the specification: ratings, size, fixing, IP rating, certification and warranty. The substitute is ordered only after the designer or client approves it in writing. Approval matters because the specification is part of the contract, and a different item may not fit, may not meet the design or may fail the inspection. Records matter because they show who agreed each change and why, they explain cost changes on the final account, and they help if a fault or dispute appears later.
markingPoints: Gets the design change in writing and finds affected orders
Amends unshipped orders with written confirmation; handles shipped goods
Compares substitutes with the specification using data sheets
Orders substitutes only with written approval, and says why
Keeps records for cost, disputes and later faults

essays.stem: Explain how ordered materials such as cable drums, boards, light fittings, batteries and solvents should be stored on site until they are used, and how careful ordering can reduce storage problems.
essays.modelAnswer: Cable drums should stand on their rims on firm, level ground, chocked so they cannot roll, with the cable ends sealed and the drum under cover or out of strong sun. Distribution boards should be kept dry, upright or as the maker says, in their packaging and away from dust, paint and building work until they are fitted. Light fittings stay boxed on shelves, not stacked so high that the bottom boxes crush. Batteries for emergency lights should be kept cool and dry, and fitted soon, as they lose charge and life. Solvent cement and cleaners are stored in a ventilated, locked area away from heat and sparks, with their SDS. Careful ordering reduces storage problems: delivering in stages to match the programme means less stock on site, less theft and damage, and less money tied up. Items with a short shelf life are ordered close to when they are needed, and quantities are kept to what the take-off shows plus a sensible allowance.
markingPoints: Cable drums: on rims, chocked, sealed ends, covered
Boards and fittings: dry, protected, not crushed
Batteries and solvents: cool, ventilated, safe store with SDS, fitted soon
Staged deliveries cut stock, theft and damage
Short-life items ordered close to use; sensible quantities

essays.stem: Explain how a maintenance supervisor at a hotel should decide which electrical spares to keep in stock and how they should be reordered.
essays.modelAnswer: The supervisor should first list the hotel's equipment from the asset register: pumps, motors, A/C units, boards, lighting, emergency lights, the generator and its changeover switch. For each, she asks how critical it is: what happens if it fails, how long a new part takes to arrive, and how often it has failed in the past. Parts for critical items with long lead times, such as a spare pump motor, contactors and overload relays for the water pumps, generator filters and fuses, and breakers of the main ratings, should be held. Common, cheap items that fail often, such as lamps, drivers, fuses and emergency light batteries, are kept in small quantities with reorder levels. Items that are easy to get the same day need not be stocked. Each spare is labelled with its part number and the equipment it fits, kept in a locked store and recorded. When one is used, it is logged and reordered at once, and the list is reviewed each year or when equipment changes.
markingPoints: Lists equipment from the asset register
Judges criticality, lead time and failure history
Keeps critical long-lead spares and common fast-wearing items
Labels, stores and records spares securely
Reorders when used and reviews the list regularly

essays.stem: As supervisor, describe a simple ordering procedure for a small electrical contractor so that orders are correct, approved, tracked and recorded.
essays.modelAnswer: Step one: the electrician or site supervisor works out what is needed from the take-off or job sheet, checks the store, and raises a numbered requisition with the job number, full description, part number, quantity, unit and the date needed. Step two: the buyer checks it against the drawings and specification and against any order already placed, then gets prices from approved suppliers. Step three: a purchase order is written with a unique number, the full descriptions, prices, delivery address, site contact and dates, and it is signed by someone allowed to approve that value. Step four: the order is sent, the supplier's confirmation is checked, and the order goes on the tracker. Step five: the order is chased as the due date comes near. Step six: on delivery the goods are checked against the order and the delivery note, and any problems are recorded and reported. Step seven: the invoice is checked against the order and receipt before payment, and all documents are filed by job number. The procedure is written down and staff are trained on it.
markingPoints: Numbered requisition with full details and job number
Buyer checks against specification and existing orders, uses approved suppliers
Purchase order with full details, approved within limits
Confirmation checked, order tracked and chased
Delivery checked, invoice matched, documents filed; procedure written and trained

practical1.title: Prepare a bill of materials and an order schedule for a small commercial job
practical1.brief: The assessor gives the group the drawings and specification for the electrical work in a small single-storey office in Mandeville (lighting, socket outlets, A/C supplies, a distribution board and containment), a store stock list, a supplier price and lead-time list (all made up) and a short job programme. As an ordering team: (1) split the job into four sections (containment, cabling, accessories and lighting, board and protection), with each member taking one section; (2) take off the quantities for your section from the drawings to scale, add drops and a waste allowance, and round to the supplier's units of issue; (3) write each line with a full description, part number, rating and unit; (4) check the stock list and deduct usable stock; (5) together, combine the sections into one bill of materials and check another member's section; (6) build an order schedule showing the order date, lead time and date needed for each line, with long-lead items marked; (7) write two purchase orders from it, ready for approval by the assessor. Photograph each stage.
materials: Drawings and specification of a small office (from the assessor)
Store stock list and supplier price and lead-time list (made up)
Take-off sheets, purchase order forms, or a computer with a spreadsheet
A phone or camera for photos
photos: The marked-up drawing for each member's section
Each member's take-off sheet with drops and waste added
The combined bill of materials with full descriptions
The stock check, showing items deducted
The order schedule with long-lead items marked
checklist: Took off their section accurately, to scale, with drops and waste
Rounded quantities to the supplier's units of issue
Wrote full descriptions with part numbers, ratings and units
Checked the stock list and deducted usable stock
Placed order dates correctly from lead times and the programme
Checked another member's section and corrected errors
Completed a purchase order clearly and correctly
safety: This is a desk task: keep bags and cables off the floor and walkways
Sit with good posture; take short breaks if using a screen
Keep supplier prices confidential within the group

practical2.title: Receive, inspect and record a mixed delivery and deal with the problems
practical2.brief: The assessor sets up a mock delivery in the store: coils and a small drum of cable, boxes of breakers and RCDs, light fittings, glands and conduit fittings, with a purchase order and a delivery note. Some problems are planted: a short quantity, a wrong breaker rating, a coil with a damaged sheath, a box of fittings with the wrong IP rating, and an item not on the order. As a store team: (1) check the delivery against the purchase order and delivery note, reading the sheath printing, rating plates and labels; (2) record every problem with a photo, and write it on the delivery note before signing for what actually arrived; (3) label damaged and wrong items and set them aside; (4) write a discrepancy report and a returns request for the supplier; (5) update the bin cards or stock spreadsheet and the order tracker; (6) store the good items correctly, using team lifts for the drum. Each member checks one group of items and records their findings, and every member helps with storage. Photograph each stage.
materials: Mock delivery of cable, breakers, RCDs, fittings, glands and conduit fittings, with planted problems
Purchase order and delivery note (from the assessor)
Bin cards or a stock spreadsheet, order tracker, discrepancy and returns forms
Drum stand or chocks, shelving, gloves and safety boots
A phone or camera for photos
photos: The delivery laid out with the purchase order and delivery note
Each planted problem, close up, with its label
The delivery note marked with shortages and damage before signing
The updated bin cards or stock spreadsheet and order tracker
The good items stored, with the drum on its rims and chocked
checklist: Checked their items against the order and delivery note
Read sheath printing, rating plates and labels correctly
Found and recorded the planted problems
Marked the delivery note correctly before signing
Wrote a clear part of the discrepancy report or returns request
Updated the stock records and tracker correctly
Lifted and stored items safely and correctly
safety: Use team lifts or a drum trolley for the cable drum, and keep backs straight
Wear gloves and safety boots when handling cable and boxes
Chock drums so they cannot roll; keep walkways clear
None of the items is connected to any supply
Follow the Centre's store and workshop rules
